{{Short description|Derivative defined on normed spaces}}
{{distinguish|Differentiation in Fréchet spaces}}
{{first-person|date=June 2026}}
{{Calculus}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Fréchet derivative''' is a [[derivative]] defined on [[normed space]]s. Named after [[Maurice René Fréchet|Maurice Fréchet]], it is commonly used to generalize the derivative of a [[real-valued function]] of a single real variable to the case of a [[vector-valued function]] of multiple real variables, and to define the [[functional derivative]] used widely in the [[calculus of variations]].

Generally, it extends the idea of the derivative from real-valued [[Function (mathematics)|functions]] of one real variable to functions on normed spaces. The Fréchet derivative should be contrasted to the more general [[Gateaux derivative]] which is a generalization of the classical [[directional derivative]].

The Fréchet derivative has applications to nonlinear problems throughout [[mathematical analysis]] and physical sciences, particularly to the calculus of variations and much of nonlinear analysis and [[nonlinear functional analysis]].

== Definition ==

Let <math>V</math> and <math>W</math> be [[normed vector space]]s, and <math>U\subseteq V</math> be an [[open subset]] of <math>V.</math> A function <math>f : U \to W</math> is called ''Fréchet differentiable'' at <math>x \in U</math> if there exists a [[bounded linear operator]] <math>A:V\to W</math> such that
<math display=block>\lim_{\|h\|_{V} \to 0} \frac{\| f(x + h) - f(x) - A(h)\|_W}{\|h\|_V} = 0\text{.}</math>

The [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] here is meant in the usual sense of a [[limit of a function]] defined on a metric space (see [[Limit of a function#Functions on metric spaces|Functions on metric spaces]]), using <math>V</math> and <math>W</math> as the two metric spaces, and the above expression as the function of argument <math>h</math> in <math>V.</math> As a consequence, it must exist for all [[sequence]]s <math>\langle h_n\rangle_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> of non-zero elements of <math>V</math> that converge to the zero vector <math>h_n \to 0.</math> Equivalently, the first-order expansion holds, in [[Little-o_notation | Landau notation]]
<math display=block>f(x + h) = f(x) + A(h) +o(h)\text{.}</math>

If there exists such an operator <math>A,</math> it is unique, so we write <math>Df(x) = A</math> and call it the ''Fréchet derivative'' of <math>f</math> at <math>x.</math>
A function <math>f</math> that is Fréchet differentiable for any point of <math>U</math> is said to be C<sup>1</sup> if the function
<math display=block>Df : U \to B(V,W) ; x \mapsto Df(x)</math>
is continuous (<math>B(V,W)</math> denotes the space of all bounded linear operators from <math>V</math> to <math>W</math>). Note that this is not the same as requiring that the map <math>Df(x) : V \to W</math> be continuous for each value of <math>x</math> (which is assumed; bounded and continuous are equivalent).

This notion of derivative is a generalization of the ordinary derivative of a function on the [[real number]]s <math>f : \R \to \R</math> since the linear maps from <math>\R</math> to <math>\R</math> are just multiplication by a real number. In this case, <math>D f(x)</math> is the function <math>h \mapsto f'(x)h</math>.

== Properties ==

A function differentiable at a point is continuous at that point.

Differentiation is a linear operation in the following sense: if <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are two maps <math>V \to W</math> which are differentiable at <math>x,</math> and <math>c</math> is a scalar (a real or [[complex number]]), then the Fréchet derivative obeys the following properties:  
<math display=block>D(cf)(x) = cDf(x)</math>
<math display=block>D(f+g)(x) = Df(x) + Dg(x).</math>

The [[chain rule]] is also valid in this context: if <math>f : U \to Y</math> is differentiable at <math>x \in U,</math> and <math>g : Y \to W</math> is differentiable at <math>y = f(x),</math> then the composition <math>g \circ f</math> is differentiable at <math>x</math> and the derivative is the [[Function composition|composition]] of the derivatives:

<math display=block>D(g \circ f) = (Dg \circ f)\cdot Df</math>

== Finite dimensions ==

The Fréchet derivative in finite-dimensional spaces is the usual derivative. In particular, it is represented in coordinates by the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian matrix]].

Suppose that <math>f</math> is a map, <math>f : U \subseteq \R^n \to \R^m</math> with <math>U</math> an open set. If <math>f</math> is Fréchet differentiable at a point <math>a \in U,</math> then its derivative is
<math display=block>\begin{cases} Df(a) : \R^n \to \R^m \\ Df(a)(v) = J_f(a) v \end{cases}</math>
where <math>J_f(a)</math> denotes the Jacobian matrix of <math>f</math> at <math>a.</math>

Furthermore, the partial derivatives of <math>f</math> are given by
<math display=block>\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(a) = Df(a)(e_i) = J_f(a) e_i,</math>
where <math>\left\{ e_i \right\}</math> is the canonical basis of <math>\R^n.</math> Since the derivative is a linear function, we have for all vectors <math>h \in \R^n</math> that the [[directional derivative]] of <math>f</math> along <math>h</math> is given by
<math display=block>Df(a)(h) = \sum_{i=1}^n h_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(a).</math>

If all partial derivatives of <math>f</math> exist in <math>U</math> and are continuous at <math>a</math>, then <math>f</math> is Fréchet differentiable at <math>a.</math><ref>{{Cite book |last=Ilyin |first=V. A. |title=Fundamentals Of Mathematical Analysis |last2=Poznyak |first2=E. G. |publisher=Mir Publishers Moscow |others=Translated from Russian by Irene Aleksanova. |year=1982 |isbn=978-93-859-2386-9 |volume=1 |pages=497-498}}</ref> If the partial derivatives are continuous in all of <math>U</math>, then <math>f</math> is Fréchet differentiable<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bronshtein |first=Ilja N. |title=Handbook of Mathematics |last2=Semendyayev |first2=Konstantin A. |last3=Musiol |first3=Gerhard |last4=Muehlig |first4=Heiner |publisher=Springer Berlin, Heidelberg |year=2007 |isbn=978-3-540-72121-5 |edition=5th |pages=394}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Rudin |first=Walter |title=Principles of Mathematical Analysis |publisher=McGraw-Hill, Inc. |year=1976 |isbn=0-07-054235-X |edition=3rd |pages=239}}</ref> and, in fact, C<sup>1</sup>. The converse is not true; the function
<math display=block>f(x, y) = \begin{cases} (x^2+y^2)\sin \left ((x^2+y^2)^{-1/2} \right ) & (x, y) \neq (0, 0)\\ 0 & (x, y) = (0, 0) \end{cases}</math>
is Fréchet differentiable, as can be seen with the chain rule, and yet fails to have continuous partial derivatives at <math>(0, 0).</math>

== Example in infinite dimensions ==

One of the simplest (nontrivial) examples in infinite dimensions, is the one where the domain is a [[Hilbert space]] (<math>H</math>) and the function of interest is the norm. So consider <math>\|\,\cdot\,\| : H \to \R.</math>

First assume that <math>x \neq 0.</math> Then we claim that the Fréchet derivative of <math>\|\cdot\|</math> at <math>x</math> is the linear functional <math>D,</math> defined by 
<math display=block>Dv := \left\langle \frac{x}{\|x\|}, v\right\rangle.</math>

Indeed, 
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\frac{|\|x+h\|-\|x\|-Dh|}{\|h\|} &=\frac{|\|x\|\|x+h\|-\langle x,x\rangle-\langle x,h\rangle|}{\|x\|\|h\|} \\[8pt]
&=\frac{|\|x\|\|x+h\|-\langle x,x+h\rangle|}{\|x\|\|h\|} \\[8pt]
&=\frac{|\langle x,x\rangle \langle x+h,x+h\rangle-\langle x,x+h\rangle^2|}{\|x\|\|h\|(|\|x\|\|x+h\|+\langle x,x+h\rangle|)} \\[8pt]
&=\frac{\langle x,x \rangle \langle h,h \rangle-\langle x,h \rangle^2}{\|x\|\|h\|(|\|x\|\|x+h\|+\langle x,x+h\rangle|)} \\
&{}
\end{align}</math> 

Using continuity of the norm and inner product we obtain:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\lim_{\|h\|\to 0}\frac{|\|x+h\|-\|x\|-Dh|}{\|h\|} &= \lim_{\|h\|\to 0} \frac{\langle x,x \rangle \langle h,h \rangle-\langle x,h \rangle^2}{\|x\|\|h\|(|\|x\|\|x+h\|+\langle x,x+h\rangle|)} \\[8pt]
&= \frac{1}{2\|x\|^3}\lim_{\|h\|\to 0}\frac{\langle x,x \rangle \langle h,h \rangle-\langle x,h \rangle^2}{\|h\|} \\[8pt]
&= \frac{1}{2\|x\|^3}\lim_{\|h\|\to 0}\left(\langle x,x\rangle\|h\|-\langle x,h\rangle \left\langle x,\frac{h}{\|h\|}\right\rangle\right) \\[8pt]
&= \frac{1}{2\|x\|^3}\left(\lim_{\|h\|\to 0}\langle x,x\rangle\|h\|-\lim_{h\to 0}\langle x,h\rangle \left\langle x,\frac{h}{\|h\|}\right\rangle \right ) \\[8pt]
&= \frac{1}{2\|x\|^3}\left(0-\lim_{\|h\|\to 0}\langle x,h\rangle \left\langle x,\frac{h}{\|h\|}\right\rangle \right ) \\[8pt]
&= -\frac{1}{2\|x\|^3}\left(\lim_{\|h\|\to 0}\langle x,h\rangle \left\langle x,\frac{h}{\|h\|}\right\rangle \right ) \\[8pt]
\end{align}</math>

As <math>\|h\|\to 0, \langle x,h\rangle \to 0</math> and because of the [[Cauchy Schwarz|Cauchy-Schwarz]] inequality
<math display=block>\left\langle x,\frac{h}{\|h\|}\right\rangle</math> 
is bounded by <math>\|x\|</math> thus the whole limit vanishes.

Now we show that at <math>x=0</math> the norm is not differentiable, that is, there does not exist bounded linear functional <math>D</math> such that the limit in question to be <math>0.</math> Let <math>D</math> be any linear functional. [[Riesz representation theorem|Riesz Representation Theorem]] tells us that <math>D</math> could be defined by <math>Dv = \langle a, v\rangle</math> for some <math>a \in H.</math> Consider 
<math display=block>A(h) = \frac{|\|0+h\| - \|0\|-Dh|}{\|h\|} = \left|1-\left\langle a, \frac{h}{\|h\|}\right\rangle\right|.</math> 

In order for the norm to be differentiable at <math>0</math> we must have 
<math display=block>\lim_{\|h\|\to 0} A(h) = 0.</math> 

We will show that this is not true for any <math>a.</math> If <math>a = 0</math> obviously <math>A(h) = 1</math> independently of <math>h,</math> hence this is not the derivative. Assume <math>a\neq 0.</math> If we take <math>h</math> tending to zero in the direction of <math>-a</math> (that is, <math>h = t\cdot(-a),</math> where <math>t \to 0^+</math>) then <math>A(h) = |1+\|a\|| > 1 > 0,</math> hence 
<math display=block>\lim_{\|h\| \to 0} A(h) \neq 0</math> 

(If we take <math>h</math> tending to zero in the direction of <math>a</math> we would even see this limit does not exist since in this case we will obtain <math>|1-\|a\||</math>).

The result just obtained agrees with the results in finite dimensions.

== Relation to the Gateaux derivative ==

A function <math>f : U \subseteq V \to W</math> is called ''[[Gateaux derivative|Gateaux differentiable]]'' at <math>x \in U</math> if <math>f</math> has a directional derivative along all directions at <math>x.</math> This means that there exists a function <math>g : V \to W</math> such that
<math display=block>g(v) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{f(x + tv) - f(x)}{t}</math>
for any chosen vector <math>v \in V,</math> and where <math>t</math> is from the scalar field associated with <math>V</math> (usually, <math>t</math> is [[Real numbers|real]]).<ref>It is common to include in the definition that the resulting map <math>g</math> must be a [[continuous linear operator]]. We avoid adopting this convention here to allow examination of the widest possible class of pathologies.</ref>

If <math>f</math> is Fréchet differentiable at <math>x,</math> it is also Gateaux differentiable there, and <math>g</math> is just the linear operator <math>A = D f(x).</math> 

However, not every Gateaux differentiable function is Fréchet differentiable. This is analogous to the fact that the existence of all directional derivatives at a point does not guarantee total differentiability (or even continuity) at that point.
For example, the real-valued function <math>f</math> of two real variables defined by
<math display=block>f(x, y) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^3}{x^2+y^2} & (x, y) \neq (0, 0)\\ 0 & (x, y) = (0, 0) \end{cases}</math>
is continuous and Gateaux differentiable at the origin <math>(0, 0)</math>, with its derivative at the origin being
<math display=block>g(a, b) = \begin{cases} \frac{a^3}{a^2+b^2}& (a, b) \neq (0, 0)\\ 0 & (a, b) = (0, 0) \end{cases}</math>

The function <math>g</math> is not a linear operator, so this function is not Fréchet differentiable.

More generally, any function of the form <math>f(x, y) = g(r) h(\phi),</math> where <math>r</math> and <math>\phi</math> are the [[polar coordinates]] of <math>(x, y),</math> is continuous and Gateaux differentiable at <math>(0, 0)</math> if <math>g</math> is differentiable at <math>0</math> and <math>h(\phi + \pi) = -h(\phi),</math> but the Gateaux derivative is only linear and the Fréchet derivative only exists if <math>h</math> is [[sinusoidal]].

In another situation, the function <math>f</math> given by
<math display=block>f(x, y) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^3y}{x^6+y^2} & (x, y) \neq (0, 0)\\ 0 & (x, y) = (0, 0) \end{cases}</math>
is Gateaux differentiable at <math>(0, 0),</math> with its derivative there being <math>g(a, b) = 0</math> for all <math>(a, b),</math> which {{em|is}} a linear operator. However, <math>f</math> is not continuous at <math>(0, 0)</math> (one can see by approaching the origin along the curve <math>\left(t, t^3\right)</math>) and therefore <math>f</math> cannot be Fréchet differentiable at the origin.

A more subtle example is
<math display=block>f(x, y) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^2y}{x^4+y^2}\sqrt{x^2+y^2} & (x, y) \neq (0, 0)\\ 0 & (x, y) = (0, 0) \end{cases}</math>
which is a continuous function that is Gateaux differentiable at <math>(0, 0),</math> with its derivative at this point being <math>g(a, b) = 0</math> there, which is again linear. However, <math>f</math> is not Fréchet differentiable. If it were, its Fréchet derivative would coincide with its Gateaux derivative, and hence would be the zero operator <math>A = 0</math>; hence the limit
<math display=block>\lim_{\|h\|_2 \to 0} \frac{|f((0, 0) + h) - f(0, 0) - Ah|}{\|h\|_2} = \lim_{h = (x,y) \to (0,0)} \left|\frac{x^2y}{x^4+y^2}\right|</math>
would have to be zero, whereas approaching the origin along the curve <math>\left(t, t^2\right)</math> shows that this limit does not exist.

These cases can occur because the definition of the Gateaux derivative only requires that the [[difference quotient]]s converge along each direction individually, without making requirements about the rates of convergence for different directions. Thus, for a given ε, although for each direction the difference quotient is within ε of its limit in some neighborhood of the given point, these neighborhoods may be different for different directions, and there may be a sequence of directions for which these neighborhoods become arbitrarily small. If a sequence of points is chosen along these directions, the quotient in the definition of the Fréchet derivative, which considers all directions at once, may not converge. Thus, in order for a linear Gateaux derivative to imply the existence of the Fréchet derivative, the difference quotients have to [[Uniform convergence|converge uniformly]] for all directions.

The following example only works in infinite dimensions. Let <math>X</math> be a Banach space, and <math>\varphi</math> a [[linear functional]] on <math>X</math> that is ''discontinuous'' at <math>x = 0</math> (a [[discontinuous linear functional]]). Let
<math display=block>f(x) = \|x\| \varphi(x).</math>

Then <math>f(x)</math> is Gateaux differentiable at <math>x = 0</math> with derivative <math>0.</math> However, <math>f(x)</math> is not Fréchet differentiable since the limit
<math display=block>\lim_{x \to 0} \varphi(x)</math>
does not exist.

== Higher derivatives ==

If <math>f : U \to W</math> is a differentiable function at all points in an open subset <math>U</math> of <math>V,</math> it follows that its derivative
<math display=block>D f : U \to L(V, W)</math>
is a function from <math>U</math> to the space <math>L(V, W)</math> of all bounded linear operators from <math>V</math> to <math>W.</math> This function may also have a derivative, the ''second order derivative'' of <math>f,</math> which, by the definition of derivative, will be a map
<math display=block>D^2 f : U \to L(V, L(V, W)).</math>

To make it easier to work with second-order derivatives, the space on the right-hand side is identified with the Banach space <math>L^2(V \times V, W)</math> of all continuous [[bilinear map]]s from <math>V</math> to <math>W.</math> An element <math>\varphi</math> in <math>L(V, L(V, W))</math> is thus identified with <math>\psi</math> in <math>L^2(V \times V, W)</math> such that for all <math>x, y \in V,</math>
<math display=block>\varphi(x)(y) = \psi(x, y).</math>

(Intuitively: a function <math>\varphi</math> linear in <math>x</math> with <math>\varphi(x)</math> linear in <math>y</math> is the same as a bilinear function <math>\psi</math> in <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>).

One may differentiate
<math display=block>D^2 f : U \to L^2(V\times V, W)</math>
again, to obtain the ''third order derivative'', which at each point will be a ''trilinear map'', and so on. The <math>n</math>-th derivative will be a function
<math display=block>D^n f : U \to L^n(V \times V \times \cdots \times V, W),</math>
taking values in the Banach space of continuous [[multilinear map]]s in <math>n</math> arguments from <math>V</math> to <math>W.</math> Recursively, a function <math>f</math> is <math>n+1</math> times differentiable on <math>U</math> if it is <math>n</math> times differentiable on <math>U</math> and for each <math>x \in U</math> there exists a continuous multilinear map <math>A</math> of <math>n+1</math> arguments such that the limit
<math display=block>\lim_{h_{n+1} \to 0} \frac{ \left\| D^nf \left(x + h_{n+1} \right)(h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n) - D^nf(x)(h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n) - A \left(h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n, h_{n+1} \right) \right\| }{\left\|h_{n+1}\right\|} = 0</math>
exists [[Uniform convergence|uniformly]] for <math>h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n</math> in bounded sets in <math>V.</math> In that case, <math>A</math> is the <math>(n+1)</math>st derivative of <math>f</math> at <math>x.</math>

Moreover, by definition of the [[tensor product]], we may identify a member of the space <math>L^n\left(V \times V \times \cdots \times V, W\right)</math> with a linear map in <math>L\left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^n V_j, W\right)</math> through the identification <math>f\left(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\right) = f\left(x_1 \otimes x_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes x_n\right),</math> thus viewing the derivative as a linear map.

== Partial Fréchet derivatives ==

In this section, we extend the usual notion of [[partial derivative]]s, which is defined for functions of the form <math>f: \R^n \to \R,</math> to functions whose domains and target spaces are arbitrary (real or complex) [[Banach space]]s. To do this, let <math>V_1, \ldots, V_n</math> and <math>W</math> be Banach spaces (over the same field of scalars), and let <math display=inline>f : \prod_{i=1}^n V_i \to W</math> be a given function, and fix a point <math display=inline>a = \left(a_1, \ldots, a_n\right) \in \prod_{i=1}^n V_i.</math> We say that <math>f</math> has an i-th partial differential at the point <math>a</math> if the function <math>\varphi_i : V_i \to W</math> defined by

<math display=block>\varphi_i(x) = f(a_1, \ldots, a_{i-1}, x, a_{i+1}, \ldots a_n)</math>
is Fréchet differentiable at the point <math>a_i</math> (in the sense described above). In this case, we define <math>\partial_if(a) := D\varphi_i(a_i),</math> and we call <math>\partial_if(a)</math> the i-th partial derivative of <math>f</math> at the point <math>a.</math> <math>\partial_if(a)</math> is a linear transformation from <math>V_i</math> into <math>W.</math> Heuristically, if <math>f</math> has an i-th partial differential at <math>a,</math> then <math>\partial_if(a)</math> linearly approximates the change in the function <math>f</math> when we fix all of its entries to be <math>a_j</math> for <math>j \neq i,</math> and we only vary the i-th entry. We can express this in the Landau notation as
<math display=block>f(a_1, \ldots, a_i+h, \ldots a_n) - f(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = \partial_if(a)(h) + o(h).</math>

== Generalization to topological vector spaces ==

The notion of the Fréchet derivative can be generalized to arbitrary [[topological vector space]]s (TVS) <math>X</math> and <math>Y.</math> Letting <math>U</math> be an open subset of <math>X</math> that contains the origin and given a function <math>f: U \to Y</math> such that <math>f(0) = 0,</math> we first define what it means for this function to have 0 as its derivative. We say that this function <math>f</math> is tangent to 0 if for every open neighborhood of 0, <math>W \subseteq Y</math> there exists an open neighborhood of 0, <math>V\subseteq X</math> and a function <math>o: \R \to \R</math> such that
<math display=block>\lim_{t\to 0} \frac{o(t)}{t} = 0,</math>
and for all <math>t</math> in some neighborhood of the origin, <math>f(tV) \subseteq o(t) W.</math>

We can now remove the constraint that <math>f(0) = 0</math> by defining <math>f</math> to be Fréchet differentiable at a point <math>x_0 \in U</math> if there exists a continuous linear operator <math>\lambda : X \to Y</math> such that <math>f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0) - \lambda h,</math> considered as a function of <math>h,</math> is tangent to 0. (Lang p.&nbsp;6)

If the Fréchet derivative exists then it is unique. Furthermore, the Gateaux derivative must also exist and be equal the Fréchet derivative in that for all <math>v \in X,</math>
<math display=block>\lim_{\tau \to 0}\frac{f(x_0 + \tau v) - f(x_0)}{\tau} = f'(x_0) v,</math>
where <math>f'(x_0)</math> is the Fréchet derivative. A function that is Fréchet differentiable at a point is necessarily continuous there and sums and scalar multiples of Fréchet differentiable functions are differentiable so that the space of functions that are Fréchet differentiable at a point form a subspace of the functions that are continuous at that point. The chain rule also holds as does the Leibniz rule whenever <math>Y</math> is an algebra and a TVS in which multiplication is continuous.
